strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: the paper identifies a genuine gap in V2A generation (appearance-driven models that ignore physical dynamics such as mass and velocity) and proposes an explicit mechanism (PPE + Phy-Adapter with residual Δ-modulation into AdaLN) to address it, going beyond prior physics-cue works (Su et al., Saad et al.) that are limited to drumstick sounds or indoor/AR settings.

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against nine state-of-the-art V2A models (See & Hear, V-AURA, VATT, Frieren, FoleyCrafter, V2A-Mapper, TARO, MMAudio) with standard metrics (FD, KL, IS, IB-score, DeSync), a user study on four aspects including physical plausibility, and an ablation study that includes an important control ('trained longer' backbone) showing gains come from physics conditioning rather than extra adaptation.

The proposed APCC metric is an interesting attempt at an interpretable physical-consistency measure, and the analysis showing existing models have APCC-Δ values frequently >0.5 while PAVAS achieves 0.378 provides evidence for the claimed gap.

The ablations (mass-only, velocity-only, direct summation vs. Δ-modulation) are informative: velocity conditioning notably improves DeSync (0.446 vs 0.480), supporting the claimed physical role of each cue.
Results are competitive: PAVAS-L beats the strong MMAudio-L baseline on most metrics while operating at the same 44.1kHz.
weaknesses: The mass estimation component relies on prompting a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) to output an object's mass in kg from video context. This is a weak and potentially hallucination-prone source of a scalar physical quantity; the claim that these estimates are 'comparable to, or even surpassing, specialized expert models' is only supported in the supplementary material, leaving a central pillar of the method under-validated in the main paper.

APCC has a potential circularity concern: the kinetic energy change used to evaluate generated audio is computed from the system's own predicted mass and velocities. If those estimates are noisy or biased, the metric may partially reward consistency with the model's own physics assumptions rather than true physical realism. Per-class correlations on only 272 impact moments across 10 classes also raise statistical power concerns; no significance testing is reported.

There is an apparent inconsistency in the experimental reporting: Sec. 4.2 states that APCC is evaluated on the VGG-Impact benchmark '(See Table 1)', but Table 1's caption says the comparison is on the VGGSound test set. The evaluation protocol and results for VGG-Impact are thus unclear in the main text.

The velocity pipeline depends on CUT3R dynamic 3D reconstruction from monocular video, whose metric-scale accuracy on unconstrained in-the-wild video is questionable; error propagation from segmentation and 3D reconstruction into conditioning (and into APCC) is not analyzed in the main paper.

The system is a heavy assembly of many pretrained modules (Qwen2.5-VL, Florence-2, SAM-2, CUT3R, CLIP, Synchformer, BigVGAN); although the authors acknowledge this, the practical benefit relative to simply fine-tuning MMAudio with additional caption-side motion text is not fully isolated.

User study is small (15 participants, 8 samples per aspect), and the deltas over MMAudio (e.g., 4.21 vs 4.04, 4.34 vs 3.96) are modest relative to the reported standard deviations; no statistical analysis is provided.

Presentation issues suggest insufficient polish: a broken demo-video link in the abstract ('Visit for demo videos.'), inconsistent metric naming ('PACM' vs APCC), and grammatical errors (e.g., 'We first filters out'), which detract from clarity and reproducibility.

KL_PANNs (1.55 vs 1.48 for VATT) and DeSync (0.446 vs 0.442 for MMAudio) are actually slightly worse than some baselines, so 'consistently favorable performance across all measures' is an overstatement.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: most V2A models are appearance-driven, and explicit object-level physical conditioning (mass, velocity) is a novel and well-motivated angle for improving physical plausibility of generated audio.

The system is carefully engineered: the PPE combines VLM-based mass estimation with open-vocabulary segmentation (Florence-2 + SAM-2) and dynamic 3D reconstruction (CUT3R) for metric-scale velocity, and the Phy-Adapter's residual Δ-modulation of AdaLN coefficients is a sensible, non-disruptive injection mechanism.

The ablations (Table 3) are informative: the 'trained longer' control rules out the trivial explanation that gains come merely from extra adaptation, and the mass/velocity individual vs. combined comparisons and summation vs. Δ-modulation comparison support the design choices.

The paper contributes new evaluation resources: the VGG-Impact benchmark and the APCC metric open a new evaluation dimension (physical grounding) that prior V2A work ignores, and the analysis of nine prior models reveals a real gap (APCC-Δ frequently > 0.5).

The method is competitive with strong baselines: PAVAS-L matches or slightly exceeds MMAudio-L on FD, KL, IS, and IB-score while adding the physics conditioning, suggesting the physics cues do not harm perceptual quality.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metric, APCC, has a circularity concern: both the conditioning signal and the evaluation use the same estimated physical parameters (mass and velocities from the PPE). Kinetic energy change at impact is computed from the model's own predicted physical values, so a model trained to be consistent with these estimates will naturally score well, and the 'ground-truth' correlation is itself built on estimated rather than measured physics. The validity of APCC as an independent measure of physical realism is therefore not well established.

Statistical support for APCC results is thin: VGG-Impact contains only 272 impact moments across 10 sound classes, so per-class correlations are computed on roughly tens of samples, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the APCC-Δ comparisons in Table 1.

Evidence for the surprising claim that generic VLM-based estimators 'surpass specialized expert models' in mass and velocity estimation is deferred to the supplementary material; in the main text this key premise is asserted without supporting numbers. Given that VLMs are known to be unreliable at quantitative physical estimation, this claim warrants direct, main-text evidence.

The headline quality gains over the strongest baseline (MMAudio-L) are marginal and mixed: IS 17.51 vs 17.40, IB-score 35.41 vs 33.22, but DeSync is slightly worse (0.446 vs 0.442) and KL is comparable. The comparison also mixes 16kHz and 44.1kHz models in the same table, which weakens the cross-model conclusions.

The user study is small: 15 participants rating only 8 audio samples, with overlapping standard deviations between PAVAS and MMAudio on most criteria (e.g., 4.21±0.80 vs 4.04±0.98), leaving the subjective improvement inconclusive.

The velocity estimate reduces each object to a centroid trajectory magnitude, ignoring direction and contact geometry, and its metric accuracy on unconstrained monocular video (via CUT3R) is not validated in the main text; the physical plausibility of the whole pipeline thus rests on components whose error propagation is unquantified here.

A 'Physics Parameter Estimator' section claims time-invariant mass estimation purely from VLM prompting, which is essentially knowledge lookup rather than physical inference; the paper's framing as physical 'reasoning' overstates what this component does.

Presentation issues reduce polish: the demo-video link placeholder in the abstract is broken ('Visit for demo videos'), and important details (VLM prompts, APCC computation specifics, diffusion block details) are repeatedly deferred to the supplementary material.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: existing V2A models are appearance-driven and ignore physical factors (mass, velocity) that shape real-world sounds. The framing of 'physical grounding' is well-motivated and clearly articulated.

The technical pipeline is well-designed: the Physics Parameter Estimator (VLM-based mass estimation + segmentation + dynamic 3D reconstruction for metric velocity) requires no supervised audio-physics labels, and the Δ-modulation residual injection into AdaLN coefficients is a sensible, stable way to add physics cues without perturbing the pretrained multimodal backbone.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: nine baselines across distribution matching (FD/KL with three feature extractors), audio quality (IS), semantic alignment (IB-score), synchronization (DeSync), a user study including a 'physical plausibility' dimension, and spectrogram-level qualitative analysis.

The ablation study (Table 3) is careful and addresses the key confound: training the backbone longer without physics conditioning does not reproduce the gains (70.19 vs 71.99 FD_PaSST), supporting the claim that improvements come from physics-aware components rather than extra adaptation. Both mass-only, velocity-only, and combined conditions are analyzed, and the Δ-modulation vs. direct summation comparison is informative.

The curated VGG-Impact benchmark and the APCC metric are useful community contributions that target a blind spot in existing evaluation protocols, and the analysis showing existing models have large APCC-Δ gaps (>0.5) is a meaningful negative finding about prior work.

Results are strong: PAVAS-L outperforms the strongest baseline (MMAudio-L) on nearly all metrics while using a comparable parameter budget, and the improvements are consistent rather than cherry-picked.
weaknesses: There is a potential circularity concern in the APCC evaluation: kinetic energy changes are computed from the *predicted* mass and velocities produced by the same Physics Parameter Estimator used for conditioning. While the metric is a relative consistency measure (correlation for generated vs. ground-truth audio under identical physical estimates), it structurally favors a method whose conditioning pipeline matches the evaluation pipeline. The paper should more explicitly discuss this and ideally include an APCC variant using independent physical measurements (e.g., human-annotated mass/velocity on a small subset).

The system relies heavily on pretrained modules (Qwen2.5-VL for mass estimation, CUT3R, SAM-2, Florence-2), and the claim that the estimators 'surpass specialized expert models' is asserted with details deferred to supplementary material; the reliability of VLM-prompted mass estimation on unconstrained video is not independently validated in the main paper.

VGG-Impact is small (272 impact moments, 10 classes) and manually filtered, and APCC is computed as a per-class correlation over these clips; no statistical significance analysis or confidence intervals are provided for the APCC-Δ comparisons (e.g., 0.378 vs. 0.536), so the robustness of the headline physics claim is hard to assess.

The physical model underlying APCC (mechanical energy lost at impact is radiated as acoustic impulse) is a simplification; factors like material, contact geometry, and coupling efficiency are ignored, which the paper acknowledges implicitly but does not quantify.

The user study is limited (15 participants, 8 samples per rating), which weakens the subjective-evidence component, particularly for the 'physical plausibility' dimension where the mean gap to MMAudio (4.34 vs. 3.96) is modest.

Presentation issues: the abstract contains a broken demo-video link ('Visit for demo videos'), and there are minor inconsistencies (e.g., 'PACM' vs. 'APCC' on page 2, grammatical errors in the VGG-Impact curation paragraph) that suggest the manuscript needed one more careful pass. Table 1 also mixes reproduced results, author-provided samples, and different sampling rates across baselines, which complicates direct comparison despite the stated caveats.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem in video-to-audio generation: physical grounding (mass, velocity) rather than appearance-level correlations. The motivation is clear and well-positioned relative to prior work including physics-driven impact sound synthesis (Su et al.) and material-conditioned generation.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: comparisons against nine recent V2A models on both perceptual (FD, KL, IS, IB-score, DeSync) and physics-correlation metrics, a 27-participant user study (1,512 ratings) including a new 'physical plausibility' dimension, and ablations covering physics features, injection strategy (∆-modulation vs. direct summation), and additional-training controls that rule out the 'just trained longer' explanation.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough: quantitative evaluation of the mass estimator on ABO-500 (competitive with NeRF2Physics using single views), velocity estimation validation on STARSS23 against a pseudo ground-truth pipeline, sensitivity/perturbation stress tests, graceful-fallback analysis with occlusion tokens, runtime profiling, and full prompt templates that support reproducibility.

The APCC metric includes sanity checks (inter-class shuffling degrades 0.378→0.655; injected noise causes progressive degradation), which partially addresses concerns about spurious correlation, and the new VGG-Impact benchmark (272 curated impact moments) is a useful community resource.

The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on VGGSound (e.g., FD_PaSST 47.38 vs. MMAudio-L 60.60) while also improving physics correlation, and the qualitative spectrogram comparisons are convincing.

Robustness design is well-handled: learnable occlusion tokens for missing objects/velocities, classifier-free-style dropout of physics tokens, and demonstrated graceful fallback to the appearance-driven backbone.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the APCC evaluation: the physical quantities used both to condition PAVAS and to compute APCC (ΔE from mass and velocity) come from the same Physics Parameter Estimator. A model conditioned on these estimates is structurally favored on a metric computed from the same estimates. The ground-truth-audio APCC reference and the shuffling/noise robustness checks mitigate but do not fully eliminate this concern; an independent, human-verified physics annotation for at least a subset of VGG-Impact would substantially strengthen the claim.

The 'physics estimation' components lean heavily on pretrained foundation models with substantial prompt engineering (Qwen2.5-VL for object discovery and mass, Florence-2+SAM2+CUT3R for velocity). Mass estimation in particular appears to rely largely on category-level priors embedded in the VLM (e.g., 'basketball ≈ 0.62 kg') rather than genuine visual reasoning about the specific object instance; the ABO-500 result may partly reflect this prior knowledge. The novelty of the generation side is also incremental—FiLM-style conditioning plus zero-initialized residual AdaLN modulation on an MMAudio-like backbone—so the paper's value rests significantly on the system-level contribution and the evaluation protocol.

VGG-Impact is small (272 impact moments, 10 classes) and per-class APCC correlations are computed over few events each; no statistical significance or confidence intervals are reported for APCC-Δ comparisons, so differences of ~0.1–0.2 across models may not be reliable.

Velocity estimation is validated only against a pseudo ground truth derived from the SpatialVLM dataset-construction pipeline (itself built from pretrained models), not against true measured metric displacement, so the claimed reliability of velocity estimates is on shaky footing.

Evaluation fairness: PAVAS-L and MMAudio-L run at 44.1 kHz while most baselines run at 16 kHz, which confounds direct metric comparisons; the authors acknowledge this but the cross-model conclusions (especially on distribution metrics) remain affected. PAVAS also slightly trails MMAudio on DeSync (0.446 vs. 0.442).

The pipeline adds substantial inference-time overhead (~9.4 s PPE per 10-s video, dominated by CUT3R) and is not real-time, which limits practical applicability; the paper reports this transparently but the cost-benefit trade-off is not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem in V2A generation: current models are appearance-driven and do not modulate acoustic properties (loudness, spectral sharpness) with physical factors like mass and impact velocity. Framing 'physical grounding' as an explicit conditioning target is a reasonable and interesting contribution.

The technical pipeline is carefully assembled and well documented: VLM-based mass estimation, segmentation + dynamic 3D reconstruction (CUT3R) for metric velocity, FiLM-based mass/velocity modulation of object-centric features, and a zero-initialized residual Δ-modulation of AdaLN parameters. The supplementary material is unusually thorough, covering prompt templates, module-wise runtime, invalid/missing-observation statistics, occlusion-token fallback behavior, and sensitivity analysis to perturbed physics estimates.

The ablation study (Table 3) is informative: the 'backbone trained longer' control addresses the obvious confound that gains come merely from extra fine-tuning on VGGSound, and the comparison of mass-only, velocity-only, and combined conditioning, plus Δ-modulation vs. direct summation, isolates the contribution of the physics pathway.

Introducing VGG-Impact (object–object interaction benchmark) and the APCC metric addresses a real gap in evaluation; the robustness checks on APCC (inter-class shuffling degrades 0.378→0.655; noise injection degrades progressively) provide some evidence the metric is not trivially gameable.

Results are competitive: PAVAS-L achieves the best FD/IS/IB scores on VGGSound against nine baselines and wins all four axes of the user study, with favorable gains on the impact-centric subset (Table S6).
weaknesses: There is a circularity concern at the core of the evaluation. APCC is computed using kinetic energy derived from the same PPE estimates (mass from the VLM, velocity from CUT3R) that are used as conditioning during training. A model trained on these estimates will naturally reproduce their correlation structure, so a low APCC-Δ may partially reflect fitting to the estimator's biases rather than genuine physical plausibility. The paper does not independently validate the physics–audio coupling with human-measured ground-truth physical quantities.

The physics model is crude. Kinetic energy drop at impact is assumed to map monotonically to spectral onset strength via a single acoustics reference [33], ignoring material properties, contact geometry, radiation efficiency, and the fact that only a tiny fraction of mechanical energy is radiated as sound. The claimed 'physics-aware' behavior is therefore a weak correlation-based surrogate, and the paper's framing overstates the physical rigor.

The evaluation of the PPE components is indirect. Mass estimation is validated on ABO (static single objects, not dynamic in-the-wild impact scenes), and velocity estimation is compared only against a pseudo-ground-truth pipeline from SpatialVLM (Fig. S1) — an expert-model-based proxy, not measured displacement — so absolute velocity reliability remains uncertain. Since APCC and conditioning both depend on these estimates, this weakens the evidential chain.

Gains over the strongest baseline (MMAudio-L, which is also the backbone) are modest on several metrics: DeSync is slightly worse (0.446 vs 0.442), KL is comparable, and the improvement is concentrated in FD and IS. Given PAVAS-L is essentially MMAudio plus physics conditioning plus an extra 30K fine-tuning stage, the margin of improvement over the direct backbone control deserves more scrutiny (the 'trained longer' control in Table 3 uses the S-16kHz model, not the L variant used in Table 1).

VGG-Impact is small and curated by the authors: 272 impact moments across 10 classes, with subjective manual filtering of 'ambiguous' scenes. This raises concerns about benchmark breadth, selection bias, and reproducibility of the curation protocol.

The user study is limited: 27 participants rating only 8 clips, comparing against 7 models. The physical plausibility axis in particular depends on whether naive raters can judge physical consistency from short clips, and no inter-rater reliability analysis is reported.

Novelty is largely at the system-integration level: Qwen2.5-VL for mass, Florence-2+SAM2 for masks, CUT3R for 3D lifting, and an MMAudio-style DiT backbone, combined with standard FiLM/AdaLN conditioning. Each component is off-the-shelf; the contribution rests on the combination and the Δ-modulation mechanism, which is a relatively small architectural delta.

Text conditioning is the VGGSound class label, which makes semantic alignment comparisons (IB-score, user-study semantic axis) partly trivial relative to models without text input, and complicates interpretation of the comparison table despite the ♢ annotation.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and underexplored gap in video-to-audio generation: existing methods are appearance-driven and do not modulate acoustic properties according to physical quantities (mass, velocity). This is a novel, well-motivated framing ('physical grounding') that goes beyond perceptual alignment.

The proposed system is complete and technically detailed: the Physics Parameter Estimator (VLM-based mass estimation + segmentation + dynamic 3D reconstruction for metric velocity), the Phy-Adapter with FiLM modulation and zero-initialized residual Δ-modulation into AdaLN, and occlusion/fallback tokens for missing cues. The supplementary provides full prompts, training details, runtime profiling, and failure statistics, supporting reproducibility.

The paper contributes evaluation infrastructure beyond the method itself: the VGG-Impact benchmark (object–object interactions) and the Audio-Physics Correlation Coefficient (APCC), with sensible sanity checks (inter-class shuffling, noise injection) showing the metric reflects real physics–audio coupling rather than spurious correlation.

Experimental evidence is broad: comparisons against nine V2A models on VGGSound, APCC analysis on VGG-Impact, a 27-participant user study with a new physical-plausibility dimension, ablations isolating physics features vs. longer training and Δ-modulation vs. direct summation, sensitivity analyses to perturbed physics estimates, graceful degradation under missing cues, and generalization tests on non-impact scenes.

Results are strong: PAVAS-L outperforms MMAudio-L on FD, IS, IB-score, and user-study scores, and achieves the lowest APCC-Δ; ablations indicate gains come from physics conditioning rather than extra adaptation, and the ablation control ('backbone trained longer') addresses the obvious confound.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between training and evaluation: both the conditioning signals and the APCC metric are computed from PPE-estimated mass and velocity. A model trained to couple audio with these estimates may be favored by the metric even if the estimates themselves are inaccurate. The shuffling and noise-robustness checks in the supplementary mitigate but do not fully eliminate this concern; an evaluation using independently measured physical quantities would be more convincing.

The 'physics' reasoning rests heavily on prompting a VLM for mass (essentially leveraging a semantic prior, e.g., 'pickup truck ≈ 1925 kg') and on monocular metric-scale reconstruction (CUT3R), whose absolute-scale reliability on in-the-wild video is debatable. The paper's claim that its estimators are 'comparable to or surpassing specialized expert models' relies on proxy benchmarks (ABO for mass, SpatialVLM's pseudo-GT pipeline for displacement) rather than true ground-truth velocity annotations, which do not exist for open-vocabulary settings.

Methodological novelty is incremental at the component level: the pipeline is an assembly of existing models (Qwen2.5-VL, Florence-2, SAM2, CUT3R, MMAudio-style backbone), with the novel parts being the FiLM/Δ-modulation conditioning design. The paper defends this in the discussion, but the architectural contribution is modest; the main novelty lies in the problem framing and evaluation protocol.

VGG-Impact is small (10 classes, 272 impact moments) and manually filtered, and APCC is computed per class over few clips; statistical significance of APCC-Δ differences across models is not reported, so the headline physical-consistency claim rests on a thin evaluation set.

Some evidence is weaker than others: the user study covers only 8 clips and 27 participants; the ablation between Δ-modulation and direct summation shows small differences on several metrics; and on VGG-Impact, PAVAS-L is worse than MMAudio-L on FD_VGG and IS (Table S6), complicating the narrative that physics conditioning improves quality uniformly.

Computational cost is non-trivial (~9.4s of PPE processing per 10s video, dominated by CUT3R), acknowledged as not real-time; the paper does not explore whether simpler, learned physics-conditioning signals could achieve similar gains.
